471.quote_or_event: “Balabalam janan : Aware of one's own strength and weakness.”
471.explanation: One of the thirty-five marks of the ideal Jain layman in Hemacandra's Yogashastra is knowing one's own strength and weakness. It sits next to far-sightedness and avoiding action unsuited to time and place.
471.tie_back: The Kural asks a person to weigh their own strength against the demands of the task before acting, and Hemacandra names that self-assessment as a basic householder virtue.
471.source: Hemacandra, Yogaśāstra, list of the thirty-five qualities of an ideal śrāvaka, as rendered in Vilas A. Sangave, 'Ethics of Jainism: Prescription of Ethical Code' (jainworld.com)
471._accuracy_note: Quoted verbatim from Sangave's secondary rendering on jainworld.com. It matches the Kural's 'own strength' but not its fourfold weighing of task, enemy and allies.

472.quote_or_event: “A householder is advised that according to his ability and environment he should proceed stage by stage and that he should observe the rules of discipline that are prescribed for each stage.”
472.explanation: The eleven pratimas, or stages of lay discipline, are climbed like rungs of a ladder: one rises according to one's ability and moves up only after standing firm on the step below.
472.tie_back: The Kural promises success to those who know what they can do and keep steadily at it, and the graded Jain path follows the same pattern of honest self-measure and steady progress.
472.source: Vilas A. Sangave, 'Ethics of Jainism: Prescription of Ethical Code', section on the eleven pratimas (jainworld.com)
472._accuracy_note: Quoted verbatim from Sangave's modern account on jainworld.com, not from scripture. Strong thematic fit.

473.quote_or_event: “A man believes himself a hero as long as he does not behold the foe, as did Śiśupāla (before he beheld) the valorously-fighting, great warrior.” … “So a novice, who as yet has not suffered pains and is not yet used to a mendicant's life, believes himself a hero till he practises austerities.”
473.explanation: The Sutrakritanga's lecture on hardships pictures eager novices who rush into the monastic life sure of their courage, then lose heart once cold, heat, hunger and insult test them.
473.tie_back: This is the Kural's warning almost exactly: many who did not know their real strength set out in a burst of zeal and broke down halfway.
473.source: Sūtrakṛtāṅga 1.3.1.1 and 1.3.1.3 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; wisdomlib.org)
473._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against Jacobi on wisdomlib.org. A near one-to-one match on zeal without self-knowledge; the Jain context is monastic endurance rather than worldly enterprise.

474.quote_or_event: In the Jain story of Bahubali, son of Rishabhanatha, Bahubali renounces the world after his contest with his brother Bharata, but at first will not go to bow before his younger brothers, who had become monks before him. He stands motionless in meditation for a year, yet omniscience does not come to him until his sisters Brahmi and Sundari tell him to get down from the elephant of pride. When he lets go of his pride, he attains kevala-jnana.
474.explanation: The story teaches that even heroic austerity is blocked by pride (mana), one of the four passions that bind karma to the soul.
474.tie_back: The Kural says that self-admiration and refusing to fit in with others bring swift ruin; in the Bahubali story it is exactly such pride that holds back a great soul until he gives it up.
474.source: Hemacandra, Triṣaṣṭiśalākāpuruṣacaritra, Parva 1 (life of Ṛṣabha; tr. Helen M. Johnson, Gaekwad's Oriental Series)
474._accuracy_note: A paraphrase of a widely told Śvetāmbara narrative; I did not check the exact sarga or wording in Johnson in this session, and Digambara versions give a somewhat different reason for the delay. The pride theme fits well, but here pride delays liberation rather than causing worldly ruin.

475.quote_or_event: “Do not get into an uneven road like a weak burden-bearer; for you will repent of it afterwards; Gautama, &c.”
475.explanation: In his sermon to Gautama, Mahavira uses the image of a weak porter who leaves the smooth road for an uneven one under his load, and will regret it.
475.tie_back: The Kural's overloaded cart and the Jain overburdened porter both teach that a load beyond one's capacity ends in breakdown.
475.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 10.33 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
475._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against Jacobi on sacred-texts.com (the refrain is abbreviated '&c.' in the original, as printed here). This is only a next-best match: it lacks the Kural's central point that many light things, piled up, become fatal.

476.quote_or_event: “The more you get, the more you want; your desires increase with your means. Though two māṣas would do to supply your want, still you would scarcely think ten millions sufficient.”
476.explanation: In the commentary's story, the student Kapila needs only two pieces of gold, but once a king offers him whatever he asks, he keeps raising the sum until he suddenly sees his folly and renounces.
476.tie_back: Kapila's mounting wish is the Kural's climber who reaches the tip of the branch and still strives higher; in both, going past the proper limit is the danger.
476.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 8.17, with Jacobi's note on the commentary's story of Kapila (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; wisdomlib.org)
476._accuracy_note: Verse and note checked against Jacobi on wisdomlib.org. Reasonable but partial: Kapila turns back in time, and the Jain point is about craving rather than overreaching one's strength.

477.quote_or_event: “Charity (dāna) is the giving of one's objects to another for mutual benefit–anugraha.”
477.explanation: Pujyapada explains that a gift benefits both sides, bringing merit to the giver and right knowledge to the recipient. He also recalls that charity is to be practised according to one's capacity (sutra 6.24).
477.tie_back: The Kural teaches that rightly measured giving preserves the giver's wealth, and the Jain definition of dana likewise sees a properly made gift as good for the giver as well as the receiver.
477.source: Tattvārtha Sūtra 7.38, with Pūjyapāda's Sarvārthasiddhi (tr. Vijay K. Jain, 2018; wisdomlib.org)
477._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against Vijay K. Jain's translation on wisdomlib.org. The mutual benefit is spiritual merit rather than preserved wealth, so the fit is partial.

478.quote_or_event: “Vyayam ayochitam kurvan : Spending in proportion to one's income.”
478.explanation: Hemacandra counts keeping spending in proportion to income among the basic qualities of a good Jain householder, next to earning wealth honestly and dressing according to one's means.
478.tie_back: This is the Kural's rule in plain terms: a small inflow does no harm as long as the outflow is kept within it.
478.source: Hemacandra, Yogaśāstra, list of the thirty-five qualities of an ideal śrāvaka, as rendered in Vilas A. Sangave, 'Ethics of Jainism: Prescription of Ethical Code' (jainworld.com)
478._accuracy_note: Quoted verbatim from Sangave's secondary English rendering on jainworld.com (Sanskrit spelling as printed). A near one-to-one match in meaning.

479.quote_or_event: “After having enjoyed pleasant seats, beds, carriages, riches, and pleasures, after having squandered his wealth which he had so much trouble in gaining, and after having committed many sins, he will, under the burden of his Karman, and believing only in the visible world, be grieved in the hour of death like the ram at the arrival of a guest.”
479.explanation: The parable compares the self-indulgent man to a ram fattened for a guest: it looks well fed and thriving until the day it is slaughtered.
479.tie_back: The Kural's spendthrift seems to prosper and then vanishes without a trace; the Jain fattened ram gives the same picture of apparent plenty ending suddenly.
479.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 7.8–9 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
479._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against Jacobi on sacred-texts.com. Reasonable but partial: the Jain warning is about karmic consequences in the next life, not about living beyond one's means in this one.

480.quote_or_event: “Tyāga: Charity is of three kinds, namely, gift of pure food (āhāradāna), gift of dispelling fear (abhayadāna), and gift of right knowledge (jñānadāna). The giving of these to others according to one's capacity is charity.”
480.explanation: Among the sixteen practices that lead to rebirth as a Tirthankara, Pujyapada's commentary defines charity as giving according to one's capacity, and austerity likewise.
480.tie_back: The Kural says beneficence must be weighed against one's resources, and the Jain definition builds the same limit into charity itself.
480.source: Tattvārtha Sūtra 6.24, with Pūjyapāda's Sarvārthasiddhi (tr. Vijay K. Jain, 2018; wisdomlib.org)
480._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against Vijay K. Jain's translation on wisdomlib.org. Strong fit on giving within capacity; the Kural's warning of rapid ruin is not stated.
